This research investigates the effectiveness of speech augmentation techniques in
improving the pitch controllability of speech synthesis models. We demonstrate
that augmenting speech datasets with pitch variations during the training phase
results in more controllable pitch for synthesized speech. We also introduce a
new method of speech augmentation called pitch perturbation, which alters pitch
ranges within speech signals. We compare the performance of three speech
augmentation methods - pitch perturbation, speed perturbation, and melspectrogram
manipulation - to assess their impact on the quality and naturalness of speech
synthesis. Our findings suggest that pitch perturbation yields better pitch
controllability while maintaining high quality and naturalness scores for speech
synthesis.

Our approach, Contrastative Spatiotemporal Object Reassembling (CSOR), is a
pre-training method for spatiotemporal object-centric reasoning. It involves
learning spatiotemporal object representations by contrasting correct
configurations with swapped object configurations in videos. To achieve this,
we developed a novel contrastive loss for video data, which drives the learning
of spatiotemporal object representations that are invariant to object
configurations. Additionally, we created a video manipulation method that allows
us to swap objects while preserving their appearance. By applying CSOR to
video-based datasets, we observed significant improvements in downstream tasks,
including zero-shot and few-shot learning, for multiple datasets.

A comprehensive investigation into various simulation parameters' impact on charged-current Drell-Yan observables has been conducted, using the SHARK generator to create reference predictions across distinct single-boson production mechanisms and a range of electroweak and QCD background processes. The study focuses on lepton-pair transverse-momentum distribution as a key benchmark, allowing for the identification of potential sources of discrepancies between data and simulation and between different simulation tools.

Telepresence robots have emerged as a viable option for remote interaction, enabling users to navigate and control systems from a distance. A recent study employed a mixed-methods approach to investigate the experience of operating a telepresence robot, involving both qualitative and quantitative surveys of remote-controlled systems. The results indicate that users distinguish between visual and navigational aspects of their experience, with visual aspects perceived as more immersive. Furthermore, users reported a sense of disconnection from the system and a lack of clarity regarding navigation and control. The study's findings provide valuable insights for improving the design of telepresence robots and inform the development of more effective navigation and control interfaces.

We examine a stochastic model for plant growth in an environment with a nitrogen supply that follows a multi-type branching process. We develop a hierarchical model for plant size based on the Cabral-Heckman law and a stochastic model for nitrogen availability. We analyze the model for a single plant and a population of plants and derive the asymptotic behavior of the plant sizes. We also investigate the conditions under which the plant sizes converge to a common value.

Mafia is a widely recognized social deduction game with extensive online presence, played with a balanced number of mafia and normal players. Despite its popularity, the game has not been thoroughly analyzed from a theoretical standpoint. This study provides an in-depth examination of the game's properties, focusing on the outcomes and dynamics for different numbers of players and mafia. Our results reveal that the game's behavior is heavily influenced by the presence of odd-numbered groups and the ratio of mafia to normal players. These factors lead to distinct distribution patterns and dynamics in the final round. Our research also identifies specific outcomes and dynamics that are unique to certain game configurations.

The existence of multiple Jupiter-mass planets in close orbits, such as the TRAPPIST-1 system, poses challenges for traditional planet formation theories. To investigate this issue, we conducted a series of simulations using the ORIGINS model, which simulates planetary formation and evolution. Our simulations show that planets of similar masses can converge to tight orbits by either accreting from the same disk or colliding and fusing together. We found that planets can achieve synchronized orbits within a few million years, allowing for the possibility of planets developing in tandem, as seen in the TRAPPIST-1 system.

The electrical conductivity of a carbon nanotube film at high temperatures has been studied using a four-point probe technique. The film, made from armchair single-wall carbon nanotubes, exhibits semiconductor behavior, with a breakdown of the single-electron approximation explaining its electrical properties. The observed conductivity follows a temperature-dependent activation law, with a significant energy gap closing at high temperatures. The energy gap value matches the semiconducting energy gap in the carbon nanotube energy spectrum. The primary mechanism driving the high-temperature conductivity is electron hopping between localized states. The activation energy of this process aligns with the energy gap in the carbon nanotube energy spectrum. The high energy gap value indicates weak interaction between carbon nanotubes in the film, resulting in localized electrons. The weak interaction also leads to the dominance of electron hopping over other possible conductivity mechanisms. The high-temperature conductivity activation energy remains stable even after the sample undergoes heat treatment at 300 K for 24 hours. The stability of the energy gap value suggests that the high-temperature conductivity is an intrinsic property of the carbon nanotube film.

Fuzzy k-means is a widely used algorithm for clustering data into distinct groups with varying sizes. However, the traditional objective function can lead to empty clusters or the overestimation of cluster sizes. To address these issues, we propose an enhanced version of the algorithm, fuzzy k-means with entropy, which incorporates entropy terms into the objective function to regulate the sizes and prevent empty clusters. The algorithm's effectiveness is evaluated through experiments on artificially created datasets and real-world data, including single-cell RNA-seq and ChIP-seq, showing improved performance in size estimation and cluster quality.

We propose an efficient algorithm for estimating parameters in mixture-of-experts models, where a distribution routes input data to separate, expert networks. Unlike existing methods that rely on second derivatives of the log-likelihood, our approach uses first derivatives to minimize the negative log-likelihood. This method is based on an adaptive form of stochastic gradient descent, where the step size adapts at each iteration. Experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms current best practices, achieves faster convergence, and improves mixing performance.

This passage provides an in-depth algebraic geometric perspective, offering a comprehensive overview of Jacobians and Prym varieties, including their fundamental properties, within the context of their abelian variety aspects and as specific types of curves, curves' theta characteristics, and their associated geometric and combinatorial attributes.

We examine the constraints imposed by the breaking of global symmetries by quantum gravity, drawing on the principles of effective field theory and holography. A critical finding is that the breaking of global symmetries by quantum gravity is limited, with the extent of the breaking depending on the volume of space and the mass of the symmetry-breaking field. This constraint is tested using a simple model based on the $\pi^2$ term in $SO(N)$ Einstein-Hilbert gravity, where we find that the breaking of global symmetries by quantum gravity is consistent with holographic bounds for $N \leq 8$. This constraint on the breaking of global symmetries by quantum gravity has significant implications for theories of quantum gravity, where it may influence the development of new theories of particle physics.

The presence of multiple sub-populations among blue horizontal branch stars in the globular cluster NGC 5286 has been confirmed through previous studies. This paper presents new findings based on photometric data from HST/ACS and UV WISE, which reveal that the ratio of blue horizontal branch stars with different sub-populations has changed over time. A comparison with the ratios of red giant branch stars from the same sub-populations shows that the ratio of blue horizontal branch stars with different sub-populations is significantly lower than that of red giant branch stars. This result suggests that the blue horizontal branch stars with different sub-populations have undergone different evolutionary processes.

The Madsen-Weiss theorem is a significant outcome stemming from the interplay between the b-principle and classical stability theorems in topology. A key feature of this connection is the use of Gornovik-Kudinov spaces, a type of metric space with a finite b-regularity, to analyze mappings between manifolds. This paper aims to explore alternative approaches to the Madsen-Weiss theorem by introducing a new concept of regularity and developing a generalized version of the Madsen-Weiss theorem. Additionally, the paper discusses the relationship between the Madsen-Weiss theorem and the parametrized version of the Walker's 2-2 corollary.

Deep neural networks' internal representations, known as features, greatly
affect their performance, making their transferability to other tasks valuable
for their reuse in new tasks. However, the transferability of features varies
greatly across different parts of a network, with early layers transferring only
basic image features and higher layers transferring more abstract and task
relevant information. In this study, we investigate the transferability of
features from different layers of a pre-trained network, VGG16, in a new task
of malware detection. We also explore the effect of fine-tuning the entire
network on the performance of malware detection. Our results show that
fine-tuning the entire network outperforms the other methods, with a high AUC
of 0.9833, indicating that fine-tuning the entire network is necessary for a new
task with a significant domain shift.

We investigated the information spreading process on networks with a specific focus on the impact of seed size. By using the Ferromagnetic Model and the Linear Threshold model within the degree-based configuration model, we found that the optimal network modularity for maximum information spreading occurs at a target cascade size equal to seed size. This optimal modularity increases as seed size increases and reaches its highest point at fully connected graphs. This optimal modularity value can be used to determine the best network structure for information spreading given a known seed size.

We investigate the properties of special Lagrangians in relation to their Lagrangian angles, particularly focusing on the convergence of these angles towards singular points. Our findings indicate that special Lagrangians can be divided into two distinct groups: one group where all angles converge towards zero, and another where angles diverge towards π/2, with no group exhibiting converging angles towards any intermediate value. Our analysis relies on the application of mean curvature flow techniques, along with a comprehensive understanding of Lagrangian geometry, including the use of Lagrangian framing and Lagrangian angles, as well as Lagrangian mean curvature flow and special Lagrangians.

The performance of a discrete-time channel model used in this research is evaluated, which the author previously introduced in a different context. The model's accuracy is assessed through comparison with a detailed simulation of a terahertz communication system over a distance of 1 km. The simulation shows that while the model provides a good approximation for short transmission links lacking amplification, it exhibits significant inaccuracies for longer, unamplified links. The analysis highlights the importance of considering the model's underlying assumptions when applying it to different scenarios.

Evasion attacks on machine learning models have become a pressing concern, with various methods developed to date. Despite significant research, there is a lack of a unified classification system for these attacks, leading to difficulties in comparing and categorizing them. In this research, we introduce a new taxonomy to classify different types of evasion attacks based on their characteristics, with a particular focus on problem-space evasion attacks. Our proposed taxonomy considers the following factors: (i) the type of data used to craft the attacks, (ii) the approach taken to modify the data, (iii) the objective behind the attacks, and (iv) the methods employed to assess the impact of the attacks. By applying this taxonomy to existing problem-space evasion attacks, we aim to provide a comprehensive overview of the various approaches and highlight the need for further research in this area.

The Ozy orchestration container is a software framework designed to automate the deployment and management of services, including configuration and resource allocation.  Orchestration is typically handled by application management systems, but these systems can be inflexible and limit the ability to fine-tune service performance.  Ozy provides a flexible approach to orchestration, allowing for the customization of services and enabling the use of specialized service management tools.  By providing a container for orchestration, Ozy enables the use of lightweight, general-purpose tools to manage services, while also supporting the integration of specialized service management tools for complex services.  Ozy's flexibility and extensibility make it a suitable choice for a wide range of services, from simple to complex.

A reentrant anomalous quantized phase is proposed, characterized by a unique "butterfly" shape in the energy spectrum, unlike the traditional Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian phases. This newly discovered phase exhibits the same topological properties as the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian states but can be distinguished by its energy spectrum patterns. The proposed phase is supported by a model that involves a finite-size cluster of 12 electrons interacting via a 1/r potential, where the ground states of different electron numbers fall into this unique "butterfly" phase, the Pfaffian phase, and the anti-Pfaffian phase in succession.

Recent research has revealed that primordial black holes can be in a state of thermodynamic equilibrium, existing within a Thakurta metric-defined spacetime. In this spacetime, which is a solution to Einstein's equations, we've discovered that the Thakurta metric-based constraints on primordial black holes remain valid, despite the black holes being in a state of equilibrium. This is because the Thakurta metric spacetime, when examined using geodesic equations, shows that geodesic worldlines are confined to specific regions, resulting in the Thakurta metric-based constraints still applying.

The confinement of dust within protoplanetary discs can significantly influence the development of solid particles and the growth of cores. To investigate this process, we conducted a study on a disc surrounding a Taurus-Aurigae star, using ALMA observations at 1.3 mm to map dust and gas. Our findings reveal that the disc's dust is confined to two distinct rings, with the CO snow line located at its inner boundary. The spatial distribution of dust sublimation temperature and grain size supports the presence of a planet with a mass range of 0.6-2.0 M Jupiter, orbiting within the gap at 60 AU. Our analysis suggests that this planet is responsible for the dust ring confinement, with the outer ring extending to its Styx and Nyx moons, located at 77 and 84 AU respectively. The confinement of dust within the inner ring is attributed to a smaller body, possibly a moon or a dust trap caused by the moon's gravitational influence. Our study demonstrates the potential for dust ring confinement to facilitate core growth in protoplanetary discs.

We investigate the relationship between the sample efficiency of robust learning and the benefits it confers. In scenarios where data is drawn from a mixture of clean and adversarial sources, robust optimization methods can achieve advantages over non-robust approaches. However, the need for model parameters may increase, and the availability of robust optimization methods might be limited. In cases where data is predominantly from a single source, non-robust optimization methods can be utilized, but they may not perform well in scenarios where adversarial data is present. In this context, a learning framework that can transition from robust to non-robust training is beneficial. We propose a framework that leverages adversarially trained models for feature extraction and subsequent non-robust training of a downstream task. In experiments involving text classification and image classification, we demonstrate that models pre-trained using robust methods can achieve superior performance when fine-tuned using non-robust methods, and that the benefits of robust training can be harnessed without the need for robust optimization.

This research investigates the existence of Bohr sets within sumsets of countable abelian groups by introducing a concept of upper Banach density that can be applied to any countable group. It's demonstrated that for a wide range of countable groups, including torsion-free groups and groups with non-archimedonic operations, upper Banach density is a suitable invariant for this purpose. Furthermore, the study provides examples of groups where Bohr set existence depends on this density, as well as an illustration of a group where density-based Bohr set existence fails.

A novel distributed optimization technique is proposed for a multi-agent optimization problem, where each agent represents a vehicle in a Transportation Network Tunnel System offering route optimization services to clients. The key innovation lies in utilizing fixed paths' related information to expedite solution convergence. The problem is initially reformulated as a regular Constrained Distributed Optimization Problem and then split into parallel, independent Convex Subproblems. A distributed solution method is developed to solve each agent's subproblem, leveraging the information from fixed paths to enhance solution efficiency. The method's performance is theoretically analyzed, and numerical results demonstrate its effectiveness in reducing communication frequency.

To enhance the resilience of multi-modal learning systems, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes knowledge modalities to compensate for missing single-modality data. This method leverages the knowledge that specific modalities contain essential information required by other modalities. When a single modality is unavailable, we utilize a knowledge modality to provide the necessary information, thereby supplementing the incomplete data. Notably, our approach does not rely on pre-trained models or any form of cross-modal pre-training, instead relying on a single model that dynamically determines which modality to use. Empirical results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on multi-modal classification and retrieval tasks.

A novel, unsupervised learning technique is introduced to automatically map Alzheimer's disease progression from healthy to severe stages using data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Index, which includes MRI scans without corresponding labels. By leveraging task-conditioned variational autoencoders, the method enables the creation of a continuous progression model that correlates with clinical staging, similar to supervised convolutional neural networks but without the need for labeled data. Performance evaluation on 1,000 MRI scans from 250 subjects demonstrated that unsupervised learning can achieve comparable results to supervised learning in distinguishing different stages of AD, with an accuracy of 0.85, using a small dataset. Furthermore, the model's ability to predict progression from healthy to severe stages in 10,000 MRI scans from 2,500 subjects showed that the unsupervised learning approach can identify clinical correlations, including earlier detection of multi-solitary lesions and faster atrophy in certain regions, such as the hippocampus, compared to others, like the white matter.

This research introduces the Backward Dropping Algorithm, a training method for supervised learning that tackles long-term dependency challenges in datasets. The method works by reversing the order of data samples in mini-batches, leveraging this reordering to enhance gradient descent and improve learning outcomes. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on artificial and real-world datasets, including the MNIST and CIFAR10 image classification tasks, where it is found to enhance performance by up to 10% compared to standard gradient descent.

We investigate the relationship between spin-orbit coupling and the Mott transition in two-dimensional Hubbard models with nearest-neighbor interactions. By using a variational approach based on the infinite projector method, we calculate the phase diagram of the model for different spin-orbit coupling strengths and carrier doping levels. Our results indicate that the effective spin-orbit coupling constant increases with doping in both the hole and electron doping regions, but its magnitude remains relatively low compared to other interaction parameters. Furthermore, we find that the spin-orbit coupling has a minor impact on the Mott transition, and its influence on the critical interaction strength required for the transition is less than 10%.

The interaction of dark matter with the Higgs field is a key factor in understanding the formation of structures within cosmology, and the Higgs portal serves as a primary means of communication between the Standard Model and dark sectors. The Higgs field's influence on the early Universe's evolution determines the initial abundance of dark matter, which in turn impacts the subsequent formation of cosmic structures. The Higgs portal also enables the mixing of dark matter with standard model particles, and the Higgs field's role in this process is crucial. The Higgs field's impact on the early Universe's evolution is investigated through the Higgs portal, and the findings suggest that the Higgs field's influence is most pronounced when the dark matter abundance is minimal. The Higgs portal's strength is constrained by considering the dark matter abundance, and the findings suggest that the Higgs portal's strength is not heavily influenced by the Higgs field's role in the early Universe's evolution. The Higgs field's impact on the early Universe's evolution is most pronounced when the Higgs portal's strength is minimal, and the Higgs field's role in this process is most pronounced when the Higgs portal's strength is minimal. The Higgs field's impact on the early Universe's evolution is most pronounced when the Higgs portal's strength is minimal.

In the context of black-box modeling, where the underlying system is inaccessible for analysis, researchers can utilize conformal prediction to generate reliable predictions with associated confidence intervals. This study focuses on applying conformal prediction to medical imaging, specifically in the domain of computed tomography (CT) scans, to assess the performance of machine learning models. We have developed an open-source Python library, available on GitHub at https://github.com/alegrosman/medical-conformal-prediction, to facilitate the use of conformal prediction for CT-based image classification. This tool integrates popular machine learning libraries such as scikit-learn and Keras, allowing users to easily incorporate conformal prediction into their existing workflows.

The RBB-NA algorithm offers a more efficient and accurate approach for modeling distorted DNA and RNA structures compared to traditional methods. This method incorporates a range of innovative techniques, such as a novel energy function and advanced sampling methods, to analyze complex systems. By using a grid-based approach to energy calculation and integrating multiple advanced sampling methods, RBB-NA is well-suited to handle large systems of interest to industry and medicine. The algorithm's performance is demonstrated through successful applications in modeling DNA and RNA complexes with irregularities, such as mismatches, bulges, and pseudoknots.

This paper introduces a revised version of range-adaptive ANS (rANS) with fixed accuracy, designed to enhance the efficiency of integer division in data compression, specifically for lossless compression of integers and floating-point numbers. The proposed rANS variant, referred to as rANS-F, incorporates a pre-determined number of bits to balance the speed of integer division with the level of compression precision. A novel approach is employed to optimize the encoding process, where the size of the code alphabet is maximized to achieve faster integer division times while maintaining a maximum error rate within a predetermined threshold. Experimental results demonstrate that rANS-F achieves faster integer division times, up to 30% faster, with minimal loss in precision compared to the original rANS method.

The dielectric properties of concrete can be utilized to assess the structural condition of bridges and other civil engineering infrastructures. To achieve this, a non-destructive testing technique based on microwave frequencies is being explored. This paper outlines a method for accurately measuring the dielectric properties of concrete by employing a compact microwave setup that utilizes both reflection and transmission measurements. The technique involves utilizing a frequency sweep to gather data across a range of frequencies. To analyze this data, a model that simulates the tested material as a homogeneous medium with specified dielectric characteristics is employed. The technique is tested using synthetic data and experimental results obtained from samples of different sizes and types.

The existence of heavy-heavy hadronic molecules, such as X(3872) and $\Psi(2S)$, is considered plausible due to their composition. In contrast, light-light hadronic molecules, like the $K\bar{D}$ system, are less understood. Recent studies have revealed that the $K\bar{D}$ system is not entirely free from theoretical ambiguities. This paper delves into the $K\bar{D}$ system using heavy-light quarkonium photo-production models, providing a theoretical framework that could help resolve these uncertainties.

This study presents a comprehensive overview of the research community focused on unmanned aerial vehicles and swarming technology. Utilizing a unique methodology that combines both approaches, we aim to bridge the gap between these two distinct fields. Our research involves analyzing the most recent publications to identify the key players, significant projects, and areas of focus within this research community. The outcome of this analysis reveals the top countries driving innovation in military drones and swarming technology, with the United States taking the lead in drone research and Europe excelling in swarming technology. The research also highlights the prominent institutions and universities driving innovation, as well as the most frequently cited projects and technologies. The outcome of this analysis provides a valuable resource for researchers, practitioners, and investors seeking to engage with the community.

The current understanding of cosmological models relies heavily on the assumption that the growth term is known, but this is not the case in practice. To improve the accuracy of cosmological inferences, a more precise growth term is required. We investigated the growth term using a machine learning approach on the redshift space galaxy clustering data from the SDSS-MAHALO and NOIRPROBE. By training a neural network with mock data, we found that it can recover the true growth term with high accuracy at redshift z=0.55. We also applied this method to real data and found that it can be used to make predictions at higher redshifts, up to z=2.3 with comparable accuracy. This suggests that the growth term can be determined with high accuracy at redshifts relevant for current and future surveys, such as DESI and Euclid.

A newly developed TM110 single-cell cavity at the Advanced Light Source has been integrated into an existing beamline. The installation of this cavity has enabled the creation of a dynamic particle optics interface that can adjust the beam phase space. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of this interface by implementing a closed-loop beam-based alignment system. The results show that the interface can accurately translate the beam position with an error of less than 1 μm and match the beam axis to a precision of 0.1 mrad.

Predicting pedestrian trajectories accurately is a complex task influenced by various factors such as motion patterns, occlusions, and real-world observations, making it challenging to replicate in simulated environments. Existing studies have primarily focused on developing models for testing, often neglecting the importance of training data. We argue that the quality of training data significantly impacts performance, and current approaches do not adequately address this issue. We propose a novel method to generate high-quality training data by simulating diverse real-world scenarios, including various motion patterns, occlusions, and obstacles. Our approach utilizes a learned model to generate plausible trajectories based on specific conditions, and we demonstrate its effectiveness in a pedestrian navigation framework, outperforming state-of-the-art methods with substantial gains in testing scenarios.

We investigate the computational capabilities of Boltzmann machines, focusing on their thermodynamic behavior and the parameter spaces that give rise to complex dynamics. By analyzing the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we establish a measure of system complexity and evaluate it in various configurations. Our results, obtained through numerical simulations, indicate that the complexity of Boltzmann machines is highly sensitive to both dynamic modes and parameter settings, leading to a complex landscape where different regions exhibit distinct dynamic behaviors and varying degrees of complexity.

A swarm of robots working together to achieve a goal requires effective distance regulation to prevent collisions and ensure a safe operating distance. In our research, we propose an approach that adjusts the spacing between robots based on the speed and acceleration of the swarm, ensuring a stable and efficient flow. This method, tested in simulations and real-world experiments, demonstrates its benefits by maintaining a safe and smooth movement, even in dense environments, without the need for map knowledge or communication beyond immediate neighbors.

The healthcare industry's reliance on blood tests necessitates the efficient analysis of numerous test results, a task that benefits significantly from automation. Our research focuses on developing an automated system for analyzing blood test images to extract vital information, including the detection of blood vessels and measurement of key blood parameters like hemoglobin and oxygen saturation levels. To achieve this, we've developed a comprehensive, real-time blood analysis system that integrates image processing and computational physics, along with a database of blood properties for reference. To validate our approach, we've conducted extensive experiments on a large dataset of images from diverse sources, including the public PH2 dataset and a large in-house collection. Our results demonstrate that our system outperforms existing solutions in accuracy and speed, with a mean average precision of 85.6% for blood vessel detection and mean absolute errors of 1.4 g/dL and 2.5% for hemoglobin and oxygen saturation measurements, respectively.

A variational approach is developed to approximate the adiabatic gauge potential, 
which is a key component of the adiabatic perturbation theory, without explicitly 
solving the nested commutators involved. A specific approximation method is proposed 
using variational parameters that are determined by minimizing the squared Frobenius 
norm of the commutators, with optimal parameters being proportional to the variances 
of the corresponding system observables. This approximation is validated for a two-level 
system and a multi-level system with a linearly changing coupling, with results indicating 
that the variational method can accurately capture the adiabatic gauge potential even when 
the system evolution time is comparable to the characteristic time scale of the parameter change.

Chromatic aberration, a phenomenon where different wavelengths of light are focused at varying distances, affects images by dispersing colors and distorting true color representation. This study investigates the impact of chromatic aberration on visual perception, particularly on image reproduction technologies. A subjective experiment was conducted to measure the effect of chromatic aberration on color imagery, and the results revealed that the distortion has a noticeable influence on visual perception. Moreover, the results indicate that the distortion is most pronounced when warm colors are affected and cool colors are affected in a radial direction, and that the distortion is most pronounced when warm colors are affected and cool colors are affected in a tangential direction.

The authors provide a detailed examination of the convergence for two infinite series - one comprising terms involving the Riemann $\xi(s)$ function and the other involving $C^{\Delta}$ functions. These series are derived from the Dirichlet and Riemann alternating series, respectively. Notably, convergence is observed even when the infinite series are considered as a whole. Furthermore, the authors establish that the Riemann $\xi(s)$ function can be represented by a convergent infinite power series.

A compact surface $\Sigma$ that is topologically equivalent to a 2-sphere and has a positive constant upper curvature bound is considered. It is demonstrated that if the Euler characteristic of $\Sigma$ is less than or equal to 2b-2, where b represents the genus of the surface, then $\Sigma$ is conformally equivalent to a 2-sphere. Furthermore, this result is proven to be optimal as exemplified by a surface with genus 1 and a constant curvature of 1. Moreover, this result can be extended to show that if a compact, orientable 3-manifold $M$ has a constant upper curvature bound and its Euler characteristic is less than or equal to 3b-3, then $M$ is conformally equivalent to a 3-dimensional sphere.

Researchers have proposed a novel concept for a future photon source, leveraging the energy from a cutting-edge laser-wakefield accelerator to generate high-energy photon beams for experiments. The integration of this technology promises to significantly enhance the energy of the photon beams, making them more suitable for cutting-edge physics research and potentially game-changing applications. A detailed analysis of the underlying physics and particle interactions has been conducted to refine the concept, which was initially outlined in a 2018 report. The study provides an update on the development of this innovative photon source, reviewing the progress made in the field and discussing the challenges associated with scaling up laser-wakefield accelerators to achieve this vision.

In a Type-I two-Higgs-doublet model with a softly-broken $Z_2$ symmetry, the model's parameters can be constrained by testing the $h\to\gamma\gamma$ process at the LHC. The research demonstrates that the lightest Higgs boson $h$ decays into photons in a manner that is consistent with the Standard Model, while also showing that the model can accommodate a non-standard $h\to\gamma\gamma$ process. The study further reveals that the constraints on the $Z_2$ symmetry's breaking parameter are more stringent when considering the $h\to\gamma\gamma$ process than when considering the $h\to ZZ$ process.

We investigate the property of key covered in data exchange settings, focusing on both local and global consistency. We demonstrate that key covered schema components guarantee the existence and consistency of universal solutions for every instance. We also show that the property of key covered does not necessarily imply the existence of a universal solution with the most restrictive semantics. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the property of key covered does not necessarily imply the equivalence of local and global consistency.

We introduce pyStoNED, a Python library that facilitates the analysis and
visualization of multidimensional regression results obtained using StoNED.
pyStoNED enables users to perform a range of analyses, including cross-validation
diagrams, scatter plots, and parameter constraint plots, allowing for the creation
of credible intervals and parameter correlations. The package is available for
free on GitHub at https://github.com/astro-UoL/pyStoNED.

The High Luminosity phase of the Large Hadron Collider offers a unique opportunity to test the existence of light feebly interacting sub-eV scalar particles. These particles can be produced in pairs at a level of sensitivity for the LHC, and their interactions can be constrained within the Standard Model. The constraints on the Luminosity LHC's discovery limits for light scalar particles are now being surpassed, and for the first time, the exclusion limits for the CP-violating Yukawa couplings of these particles are comparable to their Standard Model counterparts.
