To analyze the phase diagram, we use the Berry phase method to calculate the polar and non-polar contributions. Our findings are compared with existing literature and highlight the differences between the polar and non-polar phase diagrams.

Pre-trained language models have become the standard for natural language understanding tasks, with research often focusing on optimizing model performance.  Despite widespread use, the impact of special tokens in these models remains poorly understood.  In this study, we investigate how the treatment of special tokens affects the performance of pre-trained models.  Our findings reveal that models trained with standard processing of special tokens consistently outperform those using more advanced techniques, such as self-attention, in downstream tasks.  Our research also highlights the importance of considering token processing in model selection.  Notably, our results suggest that pre-trained models can achieve comparable performance in downstream tasks without being fine-tuned for the special tokens.  Our study provides a comprehensive analysis of the effects of special token processing in pre-trained language models.

This study investigates the evaluation of set additions using neural network models, focusing on the task of predicting the perceived value of a set of items relative to a baseline using absolute error metrics. We evaluate the performance of ResNet, ViT, and ViT-ResNet models on this task and find that the ViT model outperforms the others. We also examine the effect of using item embeddings of different sizes and find that using 256-dimensional embeddings yields the best results. Additionally, we assess the effect of using a mask token in the ViT model and find that its presence does not significantly impact performance.

We've studied the relationship between thermodynamic scaling and dynamic data from a specific type of glass-former, and we've found that it only applies under very specific conditions. This finding challenges a widely accepted idea that dynamic data should scale when plotted against a specific temperature-based variable. We've also discovered that the apparent scaling of data from another type of glass-former can be attributed to a simple mathematical relationship.

This study examines the performance of current transformer models on natural language inference, with a specific focus on their ability to handle various forms of negated information. We discover that models are less effective when faced with utterances that contain negated modality, negated scope, and negated quantification. To address this challenge, we develop a new data augmentation approach that utilizes contextual word embeddings to create negated instances from original utterances. This method significantly improves the model's ability to infer negated utterances, outperforming alternative data augmentation techniques in our experiments.

We introduce a novel attention mechanism, known as look-ahead attention, to enhance the performance of neural machine translation models. This innovative attention mechanism allows the current decoding step to consider future hidden states, thereby enabling it to make more informed predictions about upcoming tokens. To integrate look-ahead attention into existing decoding frameworks, we developed a linearized approximation of this mechanism, which can be incorporated into both autoregressive and conditional models without requiring significant modifications. Experimental results on the Wiki101 and WMT14 English-to-German translation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of look-ahead attention, yielding a notable gain in performance of up to 2.1 BLEU points.

This work involves a comprehensive study of symplectic geometry on cotangent bundles, yielding novel results and a deeper understanding of the field. By focusing on cotangent bundles, we can derive a more explicit expression for curvature weights, which are essential in defining symplectic connections. This approach also enables us to establish a direct relationship between Kähler forms and 1-forms, thereby simplifying calculations and providing a more explicit framework for symplectic connections. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the cotangent bundle geometry is versatile enough to encompass a variety of well-known symplectic manifolds, such as complex projective spaces, Grassmannians, and Stiefel manifolds, by deriving explicit formulas for their curvature weights and symplectic connections.

We've developed a method to calculate the thermal entropy of a subsystem within a three-dimensional conformal field theory (CFT) as a function of coupling. This method relies on the existence of a universal relationship between thermal entropy and coupling in the CFT's infrared limit. This relationship is analogous to the universal behavior observed in the entropy of extremal black holes. This method can be applied by simulating the CFT using lattice gauge theory and anisotropic Wilson fermions, and we've performed such simulations to examine the effects of coupling on thermal entropy. Our results show that the thermal entropy increases with coupling, and we've also observed a universal scaling behavior in the entropy with respect to coupling. This scaling behavior is consistent with the thermodynamic properties of extremal black holes.

This research presents a novel approach to evaluating Asian options through the
application of the single Laplace transforms, Laplace-Carson transforms, and
extended Laplace-Carson transforms, which are single variants of the Mellin
transforms, to derive closed-form solutions for the option prices. By utilizing
these transforms, we can directly obtain the option price in terms of a Laplace
variable, and further infer the option price in terms of time, which allows
us to determine the option's volatility by inversion of the Laplace variable
without needing time-dependent calculations. This method can be applied to both
geometric and arithmetic Asian options, and the option price can be expressed
as a power series of the option's strike price and a Laplace variable.

The Fermi Large Area Telescope has mapped the gamma-ray sky with unprecedented detail, revealing an extragalactic diffuse background that cannot be fully explained by known sources. A recent study has shed new light on this phenomenon by correlating gamma-ray data with X-ray observations of galaxy clusters, providing strong evidence for an extragalactic origin of the background. The research further indicates that gamma-ray emission from clusters of galaxies is the primary contributor to the background's observed characteristics. The findings are consistent with previous estimates of the background's intensity and the distribution of gamma-ray sources at high latitudes. The research has significant implications for understanding the background's origin and the properties of gamma-ray sources at high latitudes.

Inflation models featuring sharp features in the scalar potential are capable of producing distinct observable primordial non-Gaussian signatures. A general framework has been developed to compute the cross-correlation between the curvature perturbation and the curvature perturbation caused by a non-adiabatic pressure variation, known as $\delta\Phi^3$ and $\delta p_\perp$, respectively. This framework is then applied to two specific models: a sharp inflation model with a constant potential and a linear feature added to the Coleman-Weinberg potential. The impact of the feature on the parameter $g_{\delta p_\perp \delta\Phi^3}$ is analyzed in both models, revealing that the sign of $g_{\delta p_\perp \delta\Phi^3}$ can be determined by the background pressure at the location of the feature.

We introduce the LaViSE, a novel method that uses backpropagation to create a layer-wise explanation of convolutional neural network (CNN) representations. LaViSE generates a dense matrix that maps input pixels to higher-level features, allowing for the interpretation of intermediate CNN representations. To achieve this, LaViSE incorporates a learned embedding that represents the spatial structure of CNN layers, treated as a black box. LaViSE then optimizes an embedding for each layer that best matches the learned representation when compared to the original input. LaViSE's embedding can be learned in parallel, taking around 1-2 hours for standard image classification networks. Our experiments demonstrate LaViSE's ability to provide accurate spatial descriptions of CNN representations, outperforming existing explanation methods.

The intricate relationship between the electronic properties of cuprate superconductors at low and high temperatures is a major concern in the field. Despite numerous studies, the connection between these electronic properties remains poorly understood. This paper presents a unified model that describes both one-dimensional and two-dimensional cuprates, leveraging the knowledge that these systems share a structurally similar cuprate structure. This model enables a direct comparison of experimental results from one-dimensional and two-dimensional systems, thereby shedding new light on the high-temperature superconductivity mechanism.

This research examines the impact of travel time on the HIV care continuum, specifically on the treatment stage, using data from South Africa's Free State province. An instrumental variable analysis is employed to account for travel time uncertainty, with results indicating that a shorter estimated travel time to HIV care facilities increases the likelihood of patients initiating antiretroviral therapy. Furthermore, the study finds that patients familiar with the travel time to healthcare facilities are more likely to initiate treatment, while patients aware of the cost of transportation, but not the facility's operating hours, are also more likely to initiate treatment.

Researchers have discovered a unique phase transition in a specially designed helical antiferromagnet where a metastable skyrmion lattice unexpectedly transforms into a homogeneous magnet-free state when exposed to sufficiently low magnetic field strengths. This unexpected transformation occurs because the metastable skyrmion lattice has a lower energy level compared to the magnet-free state, despite initially forming under stronger magnetic field conditions. This unusual behavior is characterized by a complex energy landscape where multiple configurations with the same energy coexist. The study also reveals that the transition from the metastable skyrmion lattice to the magnet-free state exhibits characteristics of a second-order phase transition, marked by a distinct break in the curve of the skyrmion density as the magnetic field strength approaches the transition point.

This study enhances the capabilities of High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor Models by incorporating singular ARMA factors. The resulting singular ARMA factor models, known as S-AFMs, offer a more comprehensive framework that can capture complex autoregressive and moving-average patterns within large datasets. Theoretical analysis of S-AFMs is conducted under specific assumptions, yielding key findings that support model identification and the estimation of parameters. The study also presents a two-stage estimation method for S-AFMs, leveraging principal component analysis in the first stage and a least-squares iteration in the second. The theoretical and empirical performance of the method is evaluated, demonstrating its ability to accurately estimate model parameters, including autoregressive and moving-average coefficients, and the variance of innovations. The empirical results show that the method performs well in both finite and asymptotic settings, with the influence function providing valuable insights into the sensitivity of parameter estimates to outliers. The study's findings are further illustrated through a simulation example and an empirical analysis of the Euro area inflation dataset.

The paper examines the relationship between the fixed points of the Moreau proximal mapping with respect to monotone self-mappings on a Euclidean space and the solutions of an equilibrium problem where the objective function is convex and the constraint set is a closed convex region. It is established that these fixed points serve as solutions to the equilibrium problem provided certain conditions, including non-intersection of the monotone self-mappings' ranges with the constraints, are met. These conditions are seen to be satisfied in scenarios where the objective function is a convex L\'evy-Lorentz zeta function and the constraint set is a p-symmetric slice. Additionally, the paper demonstrates that the number of fixed points of the Moreau proximal mapping with respect to a self-bisection map on a p-symmetric slice corresponds to the cardinality of the set of solutions to the equilibrium problem under the specified conditions.

Deep learning models often rely on maximum likelihood estimation and gradient descent to achieve optimal performance, but this approach does not account for the uncertainty in their predictions. This lack of consideration can lead to overconfidence in the models, particularly when they make predictions outside of their training dataset's range. To address this issue, we propose using Bayesian methods to quantify the uncertainty of deep learning models, specifically by approximating the posterior predictive distribution of the models. We develop a novel approach to estimate this distribution by leveraging the uncertainty of the models' predictive boundaries, and demonstrate its effectiveness in quantifying the uncertainty of deep learning models. We also show that our approach can be applied to various classification and regression tasks, and that it outperforms other existing methods in terms of accuracy and calibration.

The geophysical and astrophysical processes that generate magnetic fields through dynamos are still not fully understood, particularly in regards to the impact of turbulence. This study investigates the dynamo process in a simulated solar convective zone, using a high-resolution model that accounts for the effects of energy cascade and eddy diffusion. The results reveal that the mean magnetic field generated by the dynamo is stronger when considering all turbulent effects, rather than when using simplified models that isolate specific effects. The study's findings are consistent with observations of the Sun's magnetic cycle.

The molecular outflow in the central region of NGC4945 has been studied using ALMA observations at an exceptionally high resolution. This study found that within a 2-second angular radius of the nucleus, there is an extremely high outflow rate of 6300 solar masses per year. The outflow is primarily driven by HCN and HCO$^+$ emissions, which are heavily absorbed by the dense gas in the region. This led to the discovery of a large molecular outflow extending up to 400 parsecs from the nucleus, with an outflow rate of 6600 solar masses per year. The outflow is likely powered by the starburst in the region, as there is no evidence of an active galactic nucleus. The outflow in NGC4945 is one of the most extreme yet observed in a star-forming galaxy, with an exceptionally high outflow rate and a large outflowing area.

A general approach is developed to derive a quasilinear wave energy equation that applies universally to any particle probability distribution. It is demonstrated that the growth rate of wave energy is determined solely by the rate of change of the spectral energy density with respect to the wave amplitude. This is illustrated by considering specific particle distributions, including Maxwell-Boltzmann, suprathermal power-law, and a distribution derived from the quasilinear solution for a Maxwell distribution. It is shown that the growth rate is independent of the wave frequency and wave number when the particle distribution is suprathermal. Additionally, the energy equation is modified to account for wave damping in the suprathermal case.

Semi-Gaussian likelihood models, particularly SGLMs, are versatile tools used for risk modeling and have been widely adopted. However, the standard implementation of SGLMs with variable step sizes relies on a uniform distribution of points, $K$, which can be inefficient when dealing with non-uniform data. This limitation is addressed by developing a new method to efficiently calculate the likelihood and its derivatives on non-uniform grids. The proposed algorithm, based on the concept of variable step sizes, is shown to be effective and efficient when applied to non-uniform grids, outperforming the alternative method of uniform grids with a larger number of points, $K$. The new method is then applied to a real-world scenario, estimating non-Uniform Distribution Exchangeable Processes (NUDEPs) parameters, which are used to model and price financial derivatives. The results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm can significantly reduce computation time while maintaining accuracy, making it a valuable tool for risk modeling in the insurance and financial sectors.

This study focuses on a Lyapunov inequality for operators within a Hilbert space, with its upper bound influencing the boundedness of the resolvent and the invertibility of the C₀-semigroup's left side. By incorporating spectral and resolvent estimates, we derive the inequality from the parabolic equation u_t = Au + f, with solutions in L²(Ω) × L²(0, T; Ω). Our analysis also includes the case of non-smooth domains in the Euclidean space.

A new code called MuMuPy has been created to study the behavior of dimuonium, 
which is a bound state of a muon and an antimuon. This code uses a Hamiltonian 
matrix approach to calculate physical properties of dimuonium in various states 
of motion. It can handle complex systems involving multiple particles and 
interactions, and it can calculate probabilities of transitions between energy 
states. The code has been used to make new predictions about dimuonium transitions 
in a magnetic field, and these predictions can be tested in upcoming dimuonium 
experiments.

This study develops a novel performance measure to evaluate investment managers, taking into account their absolute and relative wealth. A continuous-time model is created to maximize this measure, which is influenced by both absolute and relative wealth. A power utility function is assumed, with the risk aversion parameter having a mean-reverting value. As a result, the risk aversion parameter's behavior can be managed. The model's high dimensionality challenges solution accessibility, but a continuous-time portfolio strategy is derived using a stochastic Llewellyn-Davies model. The strategy's characteristics and behavior are examined, and a numerical solution is provided to demonstrate its effectiveness.

Green Pea galaxies are small, blue, compact objects that can be found in large surveys at relatively low redshifts. They possess distinct characteristics, including high gas content, strong emission lines, and small sizes. These features make them ideal targets for studying the conditions necessary for star formation and the development of heavy elements within small, isolated areas. A notable aspect of Green Pea galaxies is their association with Lyman-alpha absorbers, which are thought to be either the galaxies themselves or nearby objects. To gain a deeper understanding of the early universe's conditions, researchers studied 15 Green Pea galaxies with redshifts between 1.5 and 3.5, using data from the XMM-Newton telescope to analyze their X-ray properties. The study revealed that the X-ray emissions from these galaxies are primarily caused by the high-energy radiation emitted by young, distant quasars. The researchers also discovered that the X-ray properties of these galaxies are not consistent with the X-ray properties of typical Green Pea galaxies. The study's findings suggest that the X-ray properties of Green Pea galaxies are influenced by the presence of young, distant quasars.

This study examines the fermion-boson model in a complex geometry of varying dimensions, with specific focus on the $d$-dimensional complex hyperbolic space for $d \in \{4, 5, 6, 8\}$. We model the interaction between fermions and bosons as a perturbation of the free fermion Hamiltonian. By applying a generalized version of the Bogoliubov-Stratonovich formalism, we establish a fermion-boson functional integral representation of the fermion ground state energy. We then prove that this energy is a finite quantity for all positive values of the boson-fermion coupling strength, thereby providing insight into the behavior of quasiparticles in fermionic condensates composed of $sp, s$, or $so$ spin fermions interacting with $s$ bosons.

The braided Thompson's groups, denoted $F_{m,n}$ for $1 \leq m \leq n$, have been the subject of ongoing research due to their relatively unexplored nature. A key aspect of this research involves understanding the dynamics of the braided group $F_{m,n}$, particularly in relation to its action on a space that exhibits the properties of a free semigroup. A significant breakthrough in this area was achieved by Golan and Sapir, who demonstrated that the Thompson's group $F_2$ exhibits linear divergence. Building on this discovery, we extend Golan and Sapir's findings to show that the braided Thompson's groups $F_{m,n}$ also exhibit linear divergence for $m \leq n$.

Recent advancements in open-source pre-trained models for Natural Language Processing have been significant, particularly in the area of Retrieval Augment Generation (RAG) models. However, fine-tuning RAG models poses unique challenges due to their hybrid architecture, which combines learned dense representations with learned attention-based neural networks. This paper explores the difficulties in fine-tuning RAG models and proposes a novel approach that leverages the model's ability to retrieve and condition on context. The proposed method demonstrates improved performance on RAG-Small and RAG-Base models, outperforming existing state-of-the-art results in zero-shot and few-shot settings on datasets such as Natural Questions and Web Questions.

Riemann-Hilbert methods serve as a comprehensive approach for analyzing asymptotic behaviors in various branches of mathematics. This note focuses on a fundamental aspect of these methods - the application of model RH problems - and provides an in-depth explanation of how the De Branges' Helical Riemann-Hilbert problem differs from traditional model RH problems. Furthermore, the note examines the relationship between the De Branges' problem and the Titchmarsh-Widder inversion problem involving Laplace transforms, highlighting key similarities and differences between these problems.

To evaluate the performance of automatic summarization systems, a reliable reference summary is necessary. However, creating manual annotations is time-consuming and costly, so we suggest developing a qualification pipeline to ensure the quality of hired human evaluators and annotated summaries. By following this pipeline, which includes initial training, ongoing evaluation, and final verification of human evaluators, we can ensure the accuracy of annotations. Additionally, we propose a similar process for verifying the quality of retrieved summaries provided by external summarization APIs, which can impact the performance of automatic summarization systems. Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of this qualification pipeline in achieving high-quality annotations for a specific summarization dataset, with minimal investment of time and resources.

Text-video retrieval, a task that has gained significant attention in recent years, requires the development of robust video representations that can effectively capture both spatial and temporal details. Current state-of-the-art methods employ pre-trained models like 2D and 3D CNNs, but these models have limitations in capturing long-term dependencies in videos. To address this limitation, we introduce TS2-Net, a novel transformer-based model that utilizes semantic and structural information from pre-trained 2D and 3D CNNs to create high-quality spatial-temporal video representations. TS2-Net's performance was evaluated on MSRVTT, MSVD, and DiDeMo datasets and achieved state-of-the-art results, outperforming existing methods by 4% on average.

A novel method to detect composite Higgs models is presented, which focuses on rare top decays at the LHC. Specifically, the models predict the occurrence of rare top decays $t\to t\eta'$ and $t\to t\pi^0$, where $\eta'$ and $\pi^0$ are pseudoscalar mesons. These decays can be examined through the $t\bar{t}$ channel using the LHC's forward detectors, such as the ATLAS Forward Proton and CMS Forward Detector, which can detect the $t\eta'$ and $t\pi^0$ final states by identifying their associated neutrinos and the forward-moving $W$ bosons. By analyzing the missing transverse energy and forward $W$ boson momentum, the LHC can identify these rare decays.

A random graph with a combination of pure preferential attachment and uniform attachment is created by a hybrid random network (HYN) model. In this model, vertices are divided into two groups, one with a predetermined number of vertices and the other with the remaining. New vertices are added to the graph by first choosing a group at random and then connecting to existing vertices according to a preferential law in the chosen group and uniformly in the other. It's been found that the in- and out-degree distributions of HYNs are similar to those of a pure preferential attachment network (PPAN), but with a slightly longer tail. Additionally, the joint distribution of in- and out-degrees is closer to that of PPAN compared to a pure uniform attachment network (PUAN).

In the context of the Internet of Things (IoT), the coexistence of diverse technologies is inevitable, leading to potential signal interference. This study focuses on distinguishing between direct wireless signals and heterogeneous external interference in IoT systems. We developed a machine learning model using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and tested it with data from same-technology and cross-technology scenarios, using 5G NR signals and Bluetooth LE, Zigbee, and Wi-Fi 4/6 as the sources of external interference. Our results show that CNNs can accurately classify signals with high precision, and that cross-technology interference is more challenging than same-technology interference to detect.

This article explores the interaction between the Klein-Gordon particle and the gravitational field in de Sitter and anti-de Sitter spacetimes. A novel approach is developed by introducing a finite proper time decoupling method, which yields a Lagrangian and Hamiltonian framework for this interaction. This framework is then utilized to investigate the relationship between the KG particle and a random gravitational field, resulting in the formulation of a master equation. A random initial condition is subsequently applied to this equation, leading to the discovery of two novel concepts: the average KG particle and the random KG particle. In contrast to the de Sitter spacetime, which only yields the former concept, the anti-de Sitter spacetime yields both the former and a novel random concept.

Countable, locally standard measure algebras can be parameterized with a real parameter ε, where ε is greater than or equal to 1/2. To demonstrate this, we first establish that any non-zero, positive measure on a countable set is at least 1/2 when evaluated at a singleton. This allows us to construct a parameterized family of measure algebras, each with a measure μi that satisfies μi({i}) ≥ 1/2 for all i in the set. By taking the direct sum of these measure algebras, we obtain a measure algebra (Z, Σ, μ) that cannot be expressed as a countable direct sum of non-zero measure algebras. Furthermore, for any ε, we can find a sub-σ-algebra Σε of Σ such that μ/ε is countably additive on Σε, showing that the class of measure algebras is highly non-deterministic.

The parton distribution E is difficult to measure in fixed target experiments due to Compton scattering being the primary process, which has a low cross-section compared to deep inelastic scattering. To overcome this challenge, a new approach is proposed, where the ratio of Compton scattering to deep inelastic scattering is used to measure the GPD E. This approach is tested using real and simulated data from the COMPASS experiment at CERN, resulting in a reliable measurement of the GPD ratio with sufficient accuracy for a range of momentum transfers.

This research investigates the relationship between error correction and linear classification in complex high-dimensional neural networks. We demonstrate that error correction, a critical component of large-scale AI systems, can be viewed as a classification problem, where we aim to correct faulty output neurons. We examine this problem in both random and carefully designed (symmetric) neural networks. In the latter case, we develop a range of linear classifiers capable of correcting multiple neuron errors, and we show that these classifiers can be optimized using a straightforward method. Notably, this approach is more efficient than direct training of the error correction problem. Our results highlight the importance of linear classifiers in enhancing the performance of multi-layer networks, and we discuss potential applications and future research directions.

We investigate a Bose-Hubbard model with two species of bosons subject to spin-orbit coupling and inter-species interactions. The spin-orbit coupling introduces an effective momentum-dependent chemical potential, giving rise to a non-trivial phase diagram when combined with inter-species interactions. Our research reveals the emergence of superfluid phases with distinct spin-orbit-induced symmetry properties. Specifically, we find that the system exhibits either SO(2)-symmetric or SO(1)-symmetric superfluids, depending on the strengths of interactions and spin-orbit coupling. In the latter case, we observe a transition between a superfluid and a spin-orbit coupled Mott insulator. Our findings are verified through analytical calculations of the ground state and the second-order quantum fluctuations of the chemical potential.

A comprehensive, p-cyclic group representation theory is developed, with a particular focus on finite abelian pr-groups that can be broken down into a product of prime power order subgroups denoted as $C_{p^{r_{p}}}$ for each prime p present in the group. This representation is achieved by establishing a one-to-one correspondence between the group's elements and saturated chains of Young diagrams within the p-part of the group's order, known as $C_{p^{r_{p}}}$, where the Young diagrams represent partitions of the number $p^{r_{p}}$. This method is applied to the p-cyclic groups $C_{p^{r}}$, which can be broken down into a product of prime power order subgroups denoted as $C_{p^{r_{p}}}$ for each prime p present in the group. This representation is achieved by establishing a one-to-one correspondence between the group's elements and saturated chains of Young diagrams within the p-part of the group's order, known as $C_{p^{r}}$, where the Young diagrams represent partitions of the number $p^{r_{p}}$. This method is applied to the p-cyclic groups $C_{p^{r}}$, which can be broken down into a product of prime power order subgroups denoted as $C_{p^{r_{p}}}$ for each prime p present in the group.
